title: The catalogue you already own
thesis: Streamers fight churn with new content and new bundles. The cheaper lever is the library they already paid for. Every price rise makes viewers ask whether the service was worth it this month, and that question is settled on the home screen.
whyNow: Disney+ and Hulu raised prices again on 21 October. Antenna finds about 1 in 3 people who cancel a service buy another within 30 days, so the money stays in streaming and just moves. HUB Research says the service a viewer treats as their default is up to 6x harder to cancel. Being the default is won in discovery, not in the content budget.
questions: How much of a typical catalogue gets watched at all, and what happens to the rest?
What makes a service someone's default, and can discovery earn it?
Why do top-10 rows keep sending viewers to what they would have found anyway?
Cold start: what do you show a viewer who has watched two titles, or a service without Netflix-scale data?
Which numbers should a CPO track to know discovery is working?
bring: Mood rows, Because You Watched and Similar Titles; Curio, launched with Great American Pure Flix (public); Metadata Enrichment that describes every title the same way, old or new.
